narrative:
The 2024 Chicago White Sox will be remembered as one of the most historically futile teams in modern baseball history, finishing 41-121 to break the record for most losses in a single season. From the very first pitch in March, this was a club overwhelmed at every turn, outscored by more than 300 runs and unable to string together wins at any point of the schedule. The pitching staff, led by a struggling Michael Kopech who appeared in an alarming number of the season's most damaging moments, surrendered 813 runs while the offense managed just 507. It was a long, painful summer on the South Side.

April set the tone immediately. After going 0-3 in March, the Sox stumbled through a 6-21 April in which opposing hitters tattooed the roster's best arms. Bryan Shaw, Steven Wilson, and Michael Kopech all appeared in the season's earliest gut-punch moments, with Salvador Perez, Byron Buxton, and Josh Naylor delivering crushing blows. The one bright spot came late in April when Andrew Benintendi launched a two-run home run, briefly sparking hope that the offense might keep the team competitive. It was a fleeting illusion.

May and June brought no relief, as the Sox went a combined 18-38 across those two months. Kopech continued to be at the center of every storm, surrendering home runs to Anthony Santander, Mike Tauchman, and Julio Rodríguez in back-to-back weeks. The bullpen fared no better, with Jordan Leasure and John Brebbia each coughing up multi-run doubles in high-leverage situations. July was the cruelest month of all — a 3-22 collapse that included Bobby Witt Jr.'s grand slam off Brebbia, the single most damaging play of the entire season. By the trade deadline, the roster was being stripped for parts.

August was equally bleak at 4-23, though a brief flicker of life came when Korey Lee delivered a clutch two-RBI single in late August. September offered the only genuine comfort of the year, as the Sox played their most competitive baseball — 10-15 — with Andrew Benintendi homering for the 17th time and Lenyn Sosa providing a ray of hope for the future. For a team building toward something better, those final weeks offered the thinnest silver lining on a historically dark season.

chapters.title: The Collapse Begins
chapters.description: A brutal early stretch establishes the tone as opposing hitters punish Chicago's pitching from the opening weeks.

chapters.title: A Lone Bright Spot
chapters.description: Andrew Benintendi's late-April home run offers a rare moment of hope amid a sea of losses.

chapters.title: The Kopech Chronicles
chapters.description: May and June see Michael Kopech at the center of one damaging outing after another as the losses pile up.

chapters.title: Rock Bottom
chapters.description: A catastrophic July — capped by Bobby Witt Jr.'s grand slam — sees the Sox go 3-22 and officially cement their historic futility.

chapters.title: Gutting It Out
chapters.description: August continues the misery but a clutch Korey Lee single provides a rare moment of genuine excitement for the dwindling faithful.

chapters.title: Seeds for Tomorrow
chapters.description: A relatively competitive September sees Benintendi and Lenyn Sosa flash promise as the Sox close out a historic and heartbreaking season.
